new_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.* (Matthew 11:28). Wisdom has been calling this way all through Ecclesiasticus, and here she says it outright: come to me, all of you who want me, and be filled. When Yahusha (Jesus) stood in Galilee and said *come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden*, it was not a new voice. It was the same one, the Wisdom who sat beside the Maker in Ecclesiasticus 24, now speaking in flesh, and the ones he calls are the ones Sirach's Wisdom had already called, the weary who want her and have not yet been fed.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:19 — *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* The same call Yahusha (Jesus) gives at Matthew 11:28, *come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden*; Wisdom speaking before she came in flesh.

new_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *And they did all eat, and were filled: and they took up of the fragments that remained twelve baskets full.* (Matthew 14:20). Wisdom says come and fill yourselves with my fruits, and in the desert place Yahusha (Jesus) did exactly that: the multitude came to him, they ate, and they were filled. He is the Wisdom of Ecclesiasticus 24 feeding her children with her own hand, and the invitation of Matthew 11:28, *come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden*, is the same mouth speaking. Twelve baskets were left over, one for every tribe of Yashar'el (Israel), and the leftover says the feeding was never meant for that hillside alone. The scattered children of Wisdom will be gathered and fed the same way.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:19 — *all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* In the desert place *they did all eat, and were filled* (Matthew 14:20); Wisdom feeding her children, with twelve baskets left for the twelve tribes.

new_note: *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me, and fill yourselves with my fruits.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:19). *Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.* (Isaiah 55:1). Wisdom calls everyone who wants her to come and fill themselves; the prophet calls everyone who thirsts to come to the waters and eat without money. Both invitations go out to the desirous and the thirsty, and both offer what satisfies for nothing but the coming. There is no price at the door in either verse, only the call to come and be filled.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:19 — *Come to me, all you that be desirous of me.* Wisdom's invitation stands beside Isaiah 55:1, *come ye, buy, and eat*; the same free call to come and be filled.

new_note: *They that eat me shall yet be hungry, and they that drink me shall yet be thirsty.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:21). *But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.* (John 4:14). Wisdom tells the truth about herself: the one who drinks of her will be thirsty again, and the student goes back to the well as long as he lives. The woman at the well was told of water that would end that going back, because the well itself would be set inside the one who drank it. Yahusha (Jesus) is not the abolition of the wisdom that left the drinker thirsty; he is what that wisdom was drawing the thirsty toward, the Word the Torah kept sending a man back to, now a spring in him that does not run dry.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:21 — *they that drink me shall yet be thirsty.* The thirst that keeps a man coming back to Wisdom; at John 4:14 that same Wisdom in flesh sets the well inside him, *a well of water springing up into everlasting life*.
flag: Reworded the old note's point. It had Wisdom confessing a limit that Yahusha answers, which sets the Wisdom of Ecclesiasticus 24 below him; by the skill that Wisdom is the Formed one himself, so the note now reads the thirst as the appetite for more of the same Word, with John 4:14 as that Word dwelling within.

new_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). *I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.* (John 15:5). A few verses earlier Wisdom said she brought forth pleasant savour as the vine, and now Sirach tells us plainly what that vine is: the book of the covenant, the law Moses commanded as the inheritance of Jacob. When Yahusha (Jesus) says he is the vine and his disciples are the branches, he is not planting a new vine beside the old one. To abide in him is to abide in the Word the Father spoke, the same covenant Torah Sirach named as Wisdom. A branch cut from the vine bears nothing, and a man cut off from the Word bears nothing, because the vine and the Word are one.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:23 — *the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded.* Wisdom's vine named as the Torah itself; to abide in the true vine of John 15:5 is to abide in the Word the Father spoke.

new_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). *Moreover by them is thy servant warned: and in keeping of them there is great reward.* (Psalm 19:11). David spent a whole psalm praising the law of Yahuah (God), sweeter than honey, warning his servant, holding great reward for the one who keeps it. Sirach names what David was praising: the Wisdom whose memorial is sweeter than honey is *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage*. The Torah is the inheritance of the congregations of Jacob, the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God). It is the heritage, not the curse, and the one who keeps it finds the great reward the psalmist promised.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:23 — *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* The Wisdom sweeter than honey is the Torah, the inheritance whose keeping holds *great reward* (Psalm 19:11).

new_note: *All these things are the book of the covenant of the most high Yahuah (God), even the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* (Ecclesiasticus 24:23). *He sheweth his word unto Jacob, his statutes and his judgments unto Yashar'el (Israel).* (Psalm 147:19). Sirach says it without a veil: Wisdom is the book of the covenant, the law Moses commanded as the heritage of Jacob. The psalmist had already sung that Yahuah (God) shows his word to Jacob and his statutes and judgments to Yashar'el (Israel), and the next verse of that psalm says he did not deal so with any nation. The Torah is an inheritance handed to one family, the congregations of Jacob, and an inheritance is a gift to a son, not a burden laid on a slave. The law is the heritage of Yashar'el (Israel), never the curse.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 24:23 — *the law which Moses commanded for an heritage to the congregations of Jacob.* Wisdom named as the Torah, the heritage of Jacob; the word, statutes and judgments shown to Yashar'el (Israel) at Psalm 147:19.

new_note: *Many have sinned for a small matter; and he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:1). *And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: in all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that were sin.* (Hosea 12:8). Ephraim had grown rich and could find no sin in any of his labours, and Sirach tells you how that happens: the one who is chasing abundance turns his eyes away from the small matters he sinned in to get it. The gain does not remove the sin. It hides the sin from the man who did it, until he can stand in the prophet's hearing and swear his hands are clean. That blindness is what Hosea is prophesying against, and it is what Sirach is warning the reader of before it sets in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:1 — *he that seeks for abundance will turn his eyes away.* The blindness of Ephraim's boast at Hosea 12:8, *they shall find none iniquity in me*; the pursuit of gain hides the sin from the sinner.

new_note: *As when one sifteth with a sieve, the refuse remains; so the filth of man in his talk.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:4). *And shall cut him asunder, and appoint him his portion with the hypocrites: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.* (Matthew 24:51). Shake a sieve and what stays behind is the refuse; so a man's talk shows what is left in him once everything else falls through. The servant in Matthew 24 was trusted with his lord's household, and his talk and his conduct while the lord delayed showed what he was, so that when the lord came he was cut asunder and given his portion with the hypocrites. That is a sifting of the household, not of strangers; the one being sifted had been given a stewardship. Ezekiel says the same about the righteous man who turns from his righteousness, that none of his righteousness will be remembered (Ezekiel 18:24), and John the Baptist saw the fan in the Messiah's hand purging his own floor (Matthew 3:12). The sieve finds the refuse among the servants.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:4 — *As when one sifteth with a sieve, the refuse remains.* The sifting of the household: the trusted servant's talk and conduct show what he is, and at Matthew 24:51 he is *cut asunder* and given *his portion with the hypocrites*.

new_note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?* (Matthew 7:16). Sirach says the fruit tells you whether the tree was dressed, and a man's speech tells you what is in his heart. Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same test for recognizing false prophets: you will know them by their fruits, because thorns do not yield grapes. The test was not new when he gave it; the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been teaching it for generations. What the gospel does is hand it to every disciple as the way to know a teacher, so that no one has to be fooled by the costume if he will look at the fruit.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:6 — *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed.* The fruit shows the tree, the speech shows the heart; the same test Yahusha (Jesus) gives at Matthew 7:16, *ye shall know them by their fruits*.

new_note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *O generation of vipers, how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.* (Matthew 12:34). Sirach puts the two halves side by side: the fruit shows how the tree was kept, and what a man says shows the conceit of his heart. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same two things in one breath to the Pharisees, that a tree is known by its fruit and that the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart. Words are fruit. Bad fruit means a bad tree, and bad speech means a bad heart, and no amount of religious credential changes what the mouth gives away.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:6 — *so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* Words as the fruit of the heart; *out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh* (Matthew 12:34).

new_note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man.* (Matthew 15:18). The fruit shows the tree, Sirach says, and a man's speech shows what his heart has conceived. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same when the Pharisees fuss over unwashed hands: what defiles a man comes out of his mouth, and it comes from the heart. The heart is the source. Bread eaten with unwashed hands does not defile the man; what defiles him is what his own heart conceives and his mouth lets out, and the good tree bringing forth good fruit in Matthew 7:17 is the same picture. Watch what comes out, and you have seen what is inside.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:6 — *so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* The heart's conceit comes out in the mouth; *those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart* (Matthew 15:18).

new_note: *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed; so is the utterance of a conceit in the heart of man.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:6). *For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit.* (Luke 6:43). Sirach says the fruit tells whether the tree was dressed and the speech tells what the heart has conceived. Luke's record of Yahusha (Jesus) holds both together: a good tree does not bear corrupt fruit, a corrupt tree does not bear good, and two verses later, of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. The fruit is the tree's utterance and the mouth is the heart's. The wise had named the test long before; the King made it the way his disciples would know one another and know a teacher.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:6 — *The fruit declareth if the tree have been dressed.* Good tree, good fruit; corrupt tree, corrupt fruit (Luke 6:43), and the mouth is the heart's fruit.

new_note: *Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:7). *Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.* (Matthew 7:20). Sirach says do not praise a man until you have heard him speak, because that is where men are tried. Yahusha (Jesus) closes his warning about false prophets the same way: by their fruits you shall know them. A prophet's teaching is his fruit, and a teaching that voids the commandments of Yahuah (God) names the wolf no matter what signs he carries, because Deuteronomy 13 had already said the sign does not excuse the leading away. Hear him speak first; then you know what he is.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:7 — *Praise no man before you hear him speak.* The man is tried in his speaking; *by their fruits ye shall know them* (Matthew 7:20), and a teacher's teaching is his fruit.

new_note: *Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:7). *But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.* (Matthew 12:36). Sirach says a man is tried when he speaks, so hear him before you praise him. Yahusha (Jesus) carries the same trial all the way to the end: every idle word men speak will be given account of in the day of judgment. What Sirach says a wise listener does now, the Judge will do then. The words are the evidence of the heart, and the heart is what the judgment weighs.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:7 — *Praise no man before you hear him speak; for this is the trial of men.* Speech as the trial of a man; at Matthew 12:36 that trial reaches the day of judgment, where *every idle word* is given account of.

new_note: *The talk of him that sweareth much makes the hair stand upright; and their brawls make one stop his ears.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:14). *And, Whosoever shall swear by the altar, it is nothing; but whosoever sweareth by the gift that is upon it, he is guilty.* (Matthew 23:18). Sirach says the talk of a man who swears constantly makes the hair stand on end, and their quarrels make you cover your ears. Yahusha (Jesus) met a whole religion of that: a system that had ruled an oath by the altar was nothing but an oath by the gift on the altar was binding. That is the much swearing Sirach warned of, dressed up as law, a maze of oaths that let a man say anything and be bound by none of it. The teaching that hedges every oath is what the King names blind, and his own word on the matter was let your yes be yes.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:14 — *The talk of him that sweareth much makes the hair stand upright.* The much swearing Sirach warns of; at Matthew 23:18 it is a whole system of oaths by the altar and oaths by the gift, binding and not binding.

new_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Judge not, that ye be not judged.* (Matthew 7:1). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations and says the sinful man carries both. Yahusha (Jesus) says judge not, that you be not judged, and the next verse tells why: the measure you use is the measure that comes back on you. A man carrying malice cannot judge his brother rightly, because the malice is in the judgment, and the judgment rebounds. Sirach names the heart condition that has to be cleared before any brother can be weighed.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:30 — *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations.* The heart condition that has to go before a brother is weighed; *judge not, that ye be not judged* (Matthew 7:1).

new_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Then came Peter to him, and said, Adonai (Lord), how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations, the portion of the sinful man. Peter comes to Yahusha (Jesus) still counting, asking how many times he has to forgive his brother, seven? A man who is counting offences is still holding them, and what he is holding is the malice Sirach names. The King's answer pushes past the count altogether, because the heart he is forming in his disciples is the new heart of Ezekiel 36:26, the one the Spirit moves to walk in the statutes, and that heart does not keep a tally against a brother.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:30 — *even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* Malice and wrath as the sinful man's portion; Peter's *till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21) is still counting, and the King's answer leaves the count behind.

new_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). *For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.* (Matthew 7:2). Sirach says the man who takes revenge will get vengeance from Yahuah (God), and his own sins will be kept in remembrance. Yahusha (Jesus) says it as a rule of measure: with what judgment you judge, you will be judged, and with what measure you mete it will be measured back. The standard a man uses on his brother is the standard the Father uses on him. Sirach had it in the Hebrew library long before the Sermon on the Mount: the revenger writes his own sentence.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:1 — *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God).* Measure for measure: *with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again* (Matthew 7:2).

new_note: *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God), and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:1). *Now therefore, my lord, as Yahuah (LORD) liveth, and as thy soul liveth, seeing Yahuah (LORD) hath withholden thee from coming to shed blood, and from avenging thyself with thine own hand, now let thine enemies, and they that seek evil to my lord, be as Nabal.* (1 Samuel 25:26). Abigail met David on the road while he was riding to shed Nabal's blood, and she told him plainly that Yahuah (LORD) had held him back from avenging himself with his own hand. Sirach says why that mattered: the man who takes his own vengeance finds vengeance from Yahuah (God), and his sins are kept in remembrance. David was one hour from writing that sentence against himself, and a wise woman turned him from it. He blessed her for it, and Nabal died by the hand of Yahuah (God) ten days later without David lifting a finger.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:1 — *He that revengeth shall find vengeance from Yahuah (God).* The snare Abigail turned David from at 1 Samuel 25:26, *avenging thyself with thine own hand*.

new_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.* (Matthew 6:12). Sirach says forgive your neighbour the hurt he did you, and then your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. That is the petition Yahusha (Jesus) taught his disciples to pray, forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors, and the condition is the same in both. Pardon received and pardon extended are named in one breath, in the same act of prayer. The disciples' prayer was not a new idea in Yashar'el (Israel); the wise had been teaching sons to pray this way for generations.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:2 — *so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* Forgiveness asked for and forgiveness given in one prayer; *forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors* (Matthew 6:12).

new_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *Yahusha (Jesus) saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.* (Matthew 18:22). Sirach says forgive your neighbour, and your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. Peter asks how many times, and Yahusha (Jesus) answers seventy times seven, then tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven a fortune and would not forgive a few pence, and closes it with the warning that the heavenly Father will do the same to anyone who does not forgive his brother from the heart. The Lord's Prayer had already made the same condition, forgive and be forgiven, forgive not and be not forgiven (Matthew 6:14–15). Sirach said it in one line; the King said it in a prayer, a number, and a story, and it is one teaching.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:2 — *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you.* The one line behind the King's *seventy times seven* (Matthew 18:22) and the parable that follows it: forgive, and be forgiven.

new_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.* (Matthew 22:39). Sirach says forgive your neighbour the hurt he did you, and your own sins will be forgiven. Yahusha (Jesus) names the second great commandment as love your neighbour as yourself, quoting Leviticus 19:18, and that verse in the Torah begins by forbidding vengeance and grudges before it ever says love. Forgiving the hurt is what loving the neighbour looks like when he has wronged you. Sirach is not adding to the commandment; he is reading it, and the King's answer to the lawyer stands on the same verse.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:2 — *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you.* Forgiving the hurt is love of neighbour in practice; *thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself* (Matthew 22:39) begins in Leviticus 19:18 with no vengeance and no grudge.

new_note: *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:3). *Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?* (Matthew 18:33). Sirach asks the plain question: a man holds hatred against another man, and he goes looking for pardon from Yahuah (God)? The parable in Matthew 18 puts that man in a story. He has just been forgiven everything he owed, and he takes his fellow servant by the throat over a trifle, and his lord asks him the very question Sirach asked, should you not have had compassion as I had pity on you? The pardon he had received was taken back. Mercy received has to become mercy given, or it does not stay.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:3 — *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?.* Sirach's question is the lord's question at Matthew 18:33, *shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant*; the pardon that was not passed on was taken back.

new_note: *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:4). *But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.* (Matthew 6:15). Sirach presses the question down to the heart: a man shows no mercy to another man, one made like himself, and then asks forgiveness for his own sins? Yahusha (Jesus) answers it in the Sermon: if you forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours. The brother who is like you is the test. The heart that withholds mercy from him has no standing to ask it from the Father, and the wise in Yashar'el (Israel) had been saying so long before the disciples' prayer was taught.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:4 — *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself.* No mercy to the man like yourself, no forgiveness to ask; *if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive* (Matthew 6:15).

new_note: *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself: and does he ask forgiveness of his own sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:4). *Then came Peter to him, and said, Adonai (Lord), how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21). Peter's question is about a brother, a man like himself, sinning against him over and over. Sirach had already asked what becomes of a man who shows no mercy to one made like himself and then asks forgiveness for his own sins. Peter is standing right at that question, counting toward a limit, and the King's answer in the next verse takes the limit away. The mercy owed to an equal is the mercy Sirach demands, and it is the mercy a disciple must give before he asks his own.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:4 — *He sheweth no mercy to a man, which is like himself.* Peter's *how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him?* (Matthew 18:21) stands right at Sirach's question about mercy to the man like yourself.

new_note: *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:5). *Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother’s eye.* (Matthew 7:5). Sirach asks who will plead for the pardon of a man who is only flesh and yet nurses hatred. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the man with the beam in his own eye to get it out first, and then he will see clearly to help his brother with the mote. The two belong together: the one nursing hatred cannot ask the Father's pardon for himself, and so he cannot rightly help a brother with his fault either. The beam comes out first, and the hatred is the beam.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:5 — *If he that is but flesh nourish hatred, who will intreat for pardon of his sins?.* The beam that comes out first (Matthew 7:5); hatred nursed in the heart leaves no one to plead for the man's own pardon.

new_note: *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:7). *So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.* (Matthew 18:35). Sirach says two things in one line and means them as one: remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour; remember the covenant of the Highest, and overlook ignorance. Yahusha (Jesus) ends the parable of the unforgiving servant on the same note, that the heavenly Father will deal the same way with anyone who does not forgive his brother from the heart. Remembering the Torah and forgiving the brother are not two different religions; the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) is what produces a heart without malice. And the parable is plain that the forgiveness a man received can be taken back if he will not extend it; the door home stays a door, and the man who bears malice against his brother has walked away from it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:7 — *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour.* Torah remembered and malice laid down as one thing; at Matthew 18:35 the Father deals the same way with the one who will not forgive *from your hearts*.

new_note: *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:7). *On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.* (Matthew 22:40). Sirach binds the commandments and the covenant together with bearing no malice and overlooking ignorance, all in one breath. When Yahusha (Jesus) says all the law and the prophets hang on loving Yahuah (God) and loving your neighbour, he is doing the same thing, not the opposite: he is saying what the whole Torah is for, not cutting it down to two lines. A man cannot hang a coat on a peg and then throw the coat away. Remember the commandments, and the love of the neighbour is what keeping them looks like; the heart Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26–27 promise is the heart that does both at once.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:7 — *remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* Commandments and covenant held together with no malice; at Matthew 22:40 the law and the prophets hang on love, which gathers them up rather than shrinking them.

new_note: *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:7). *But if he be shameless and persisteth in his wrong-doing, even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to Elohim (God) the avenging.* (Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs 100:7). Sirach says remember the commandments and bear no malice to your neighbour, and overlook what was done in ignorance. The patriarch's testament goes further down the same road: even if the man is shameless and keeps on in his wrong, forgive him from the heart and leave the avenging to Elohim (God). Both are the commandment of Leviticus 19:18 lived out, no vengeance and no grudge. Forgiving the shameless is simply bearing no malice when it costs the most.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:7 — *Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to your neighbour.* No malice rooted in the commandments; the Testaments say *even so forgive him from the heart, and leave to Elohim (God) the avenging*.

new_note: *He that is merciful will lend to his neighbour; and he that strengtheneth his hand keepeth the commandments.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:1). *And he said unto him, Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, Elohim (God): but if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments.* (Matthew 19:17). Sirach says the merciful man lends to his neighbour, and the one who strengthens his hand keeps the commandments; mercy and commandment are one act. Yahusha (Jesus) tells the young man who asks about life to keep the commandments, and when the young man says he has kept them all, the King tests him with the poor: sell and give. The test did not change the subject. Mercy to the neighbour is what keeping the commandments looks like with a full purse in hand, and the young man's grief showed where his keeping had stopped. Sirach would have told him the same thing.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:1 — *he that strengtheneth his hand keepeth the commandments.* Mercy to the neighbour as commandment keeping; *if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments* (Matthew 19:17), and the test that followed was the poor.

new_note: *Lend to your neighbour in time of his need, and pay you your neighbour again in due season.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:2). *Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.* (Matthew 5:42). Sirach says lend to your neighbour when he needs it, and pay back your neighbour when the time comes. Yahusha (Jesus) on the mount says give to him who asks, and do not turn away the one who wants to borrow. The Sermon takes Sirach's line and opens the hand wider, but it is the same hand. Lending to a neighbour in his need was already the commandment in Yashar'el (Israel); the King was telling his disciples to keep it without flinching.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:2 — *Lend to your neighbour in time of his need.* The open hand of Matthew 5:42, *from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away*, is Sirach's lending to the neighbour in his need.

new_note: *Help the poor for the commandment’s sake, and turn him not away because of his poverty.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:9). *And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.* (Matthew 25:40). Sirach says help the poor because the commandment says so, and do not turn him away because he is poor. At the judgment the King says that whatever was done to the least of his brethren was done to him. The mercy Sirach commands is not a charity program; it is the commandment kept, and the King counts it as done to himself because the least of these are his own kin, his brethren, the household of Yashar'el (Israel) scattered and poor. Help the poor for the commandment's sake and you have served the King without knowing his face.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:9 — *Help the poor for the commandment’s sake, and turn him not away.* Mercy as the commandment kept; at Matthew 25:40 what was done *unto one of the least of these my brethren* was done to the King.

new_note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:11). *But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal:* (Matthew 6:20). Sirach says lay up your treasure the way the commandments of the Most High direct, and it will profit you more than gold. Yahusha (Jesus) says lay up for yourselves treasure in heaven, where moth and rust and thieves cannot reach. The two are the same counsel: the hand that opens to the brother and the poor because the commandment says so is laying up the treasure the King means. The treasure in heaven is kept by keeping the commandments on earth.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:11 — *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High.* The treasure laid up by the open hand of the commandment keeper is the *treasures in heaven* of Matthew 6:20.

new_note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:11). *Yahusha (Jesus) said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.* (Matthew 19:21). Sirach says lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it will outprofit gold. Yahusha (Jesus) says it to the young man who has kept the commandments from his youth: sell, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. The King's word was a test for one heart, not a command that every disciple become penniless; it found the place where this man's love of neighbour stopped, which was his own possessions. Giving to the poor was never new; the Torah had always commanded it (Deuteronomy 15:7–8), and Sirach is only saying that treasure laid up that way is the kind that lasts.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:11 — *and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* The treasure laid up by the commandments is the *treasure in heaven* the King offers the young man at Matthew 19:21.

new_note: *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High, and it shall bring you more profit than gold.* (Ecclesiasticus 29:11). *Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.* (Luke 12:33). Sirach says lay up your treasure the way the commandments of the Most High direct, and it will profit you more than gold; two verses earlier he said help the poor for the commandment's sake. Yahusha (Jesus) says sell, give alms, and provide yourselves bags that do not wear out, a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. The treasure of the man who opens his hand because the commandment says so is laid up where gold cannot go and thieves cannot follow. That is why it outlasts gold.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 29:11 — *Lay up your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High.* The commandment keeper's treasure is the *treasure in the heavens that faileth not* of Luke 12:33, laid up by alms.

new_note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:5). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says the man who loves gold will not be justified. Yahusha (Jesus) says why: no man can serve two masters, and you cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon. The man whose heart holds to gold has already given his service to another master, and he cannot stand justified before a Father whose service is the whole heart. The gold-lover and the mammon-server are the same man seen from two sides.

new_note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:5). *And Yahusha (Jesus) looked round about, and saith unto his disciples, How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of Elohim (God)!* (Mark 10:23). Sirach says the man who loves gold will not be justified. Yahusha (Jesus) looks round at his disciples after the rich young man walks away and says how hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of Elohim (God). It is the same man in both verses: the one Sirach says will not be justified is the one the King says hardly enters. Not because riches are a sin, but because gold tends to own the man who has it, and a man owned by gold does not come in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:5 — *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption.* The one Sirach says will not be justified is the one who *hardly* enters the kingdom at Mark 10:23.

new_note: *He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:5). *No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Luke 16:13). Sirach says the man who loves gold will not be justified. Luke sets the King's verdict at the end of the parable of the unjust steward, a story about using mammon shrewdly before the books are called, and then closes it: you cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon. The divided heart that holds to gold has chosen its master, and Sirach already said where that leaves it. The setting is different from the Sermon on the Mount, but the verdict is the same, and it was the wisdom of Yashar'el (Israel) before the King spoke it.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:5 — *he that followeth corruption shall have enough thereof.* Gold-love disqualifies; at Luke 16:13 the King closes the steward parable with *ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon*.

new_note: *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* (Ecclesiasticus 31:6). *No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve Elohim (God) and mammon.* (Matthew 6:24). Sirach says gold has ruined many, and their destruction was right there with it. Yahusha (Jesus) sets the choice before his disciples: Elohim (God) or mammon, one master or the other, never both. The disciple who chooses mammon is walking toward the ruin Sirach had already watched overtake many. The wise saw where gold leads; the King made the fork in the road plain.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 31:6 — *Gold has been the ruin of many, and their destruction was present.* Where gold leads; the choice between Elohim (God) and mammon at Matthew 6:24 is the fork before that ruin.
